title: gpu-stream-nvlink-jitter-mapping
content:
Purpose / tl;dr:
- Trying to map a recurring p95/p99 jitter that shows up only for mid-to-large sequence requests (>256 tokens) on our multi-GPU Dedicated hosts. Suspect NVLink/cross-GPU memcpy stall + GPU stream serialization.

Experiment summary:
- Workload: production-like chat generation (causal LM) using model variant rdx-7b-int8 on 4xA100-40GB with NVLink mesh.
- Traffic mix: 60% single-token stepups (streaming), 40% full-sequence generation (non-streaming). We captured ~10k traces over 48h.
- Instrumentation: custom trace spans (client->ingress->tokenize->compile->kv-cache-lookup->kernel-dispatch->nvlink-copy->emit->egress), CUPTI kernel timestamps, perf counters for PCIe/NVLink traffic, grpc server histograms, and kernel queue depth metrics from runtime.
- Baseline config: runtime@main@2026-01-31, CUDA 12.1, driver 525.xx, NCCL 2.18, kernel fusion enabled, async-batcher on.

High-level findings (summary):
- Overall e2e (ingress->egress) medians: p50=46ms, p95=163ms, p99=324ms for seqlen bucket 256-1024 (batch size 1-4 mix).
- Two distinct sources of extra latency visible at p95+:
  1) NVLink copy stalls (dominant in ~42% of p95 traces): extra 25-200ms depending on contention pattern.
  2) GPU stream serialization / kernel dispatch stalls (dominant in ~38% of p95 traces): extra 15-90ms, often shows as series of small stalls across multiple kernels.
- Remaining p95 tail (~20%) attributable to OS scheduling/CPU-side stalls (rpc thread exhaustion / NUMA mis-affinity) and rare memory GC in Python model loader.

Per-stage breakdown (median and tail patterns, representative bucket seqlen 512):
- ingress (parse+auth): median 3.2ms, p95 6.1ms, p99 9.0ms
- tokenize: median 1.7ms, p95 3.8ms, p99 6.4ms
- compile/checkpoint lookup: median 4.5ms, p95 5.8ms, p99 11.2ms
- kv-cache lookup (in-memory): median 0.9ms, p95 2.3ms, p99 5.6ms
- kernel dispatch (submit to GPU queue): median 6.1ms, p95 35.2ms, p99 78.9ms (bimodal at p95)
- inter-GPU copy (nvlink H2D / peer-to-peer): median 2.2ms, p95 48.0ms, p99 190ms (heavy tail)
- incremental emit + serializer: median 4.0ms, p95 9.0ms, p99 16.5ms
- egress (network send): median 2.0ms, p95 4.8ms, p99 8.2ms

Notes on the bimodal/long tail behavior:
- Kernel dispatch times show a bimodal distribution: one mode around 5-8ms (normal), another mode ~30-80ms. Looking at traces, when kernel-dispatch enters the slow mode it is often preceded by an inter-GPU copy spike (large nvlink copy). Sequence: kernel A runs -> nvlink copy scheduled -> kernel B submission sees GPU stream busy + runtime backpressure -> serialization and queue buildup.
- NVLink copy spikes correlate with concurrent workloads on neighboring partitions (we observed NVLink util spikes when other pods on host were doing heavy D2H/H2D or NCCL allreduce). This indicates cross-tenant interference (even within Dedicated host, some shared NVLink fabric resources appear oversubscribed for certain patterns).

Deep dive evidence (representative trace snippets):
- Trace A (p50): kernel-submit 6.3ms -> nvcopy 2.1ms -> kernel-run 3.2ms -> emit 3.9ms -> total 42ms.
- Trace B (p95): kernel-submit 37.8ms (split: 28ms wait on stream + 9.8ms actual dispatch) -> nvcopy 67.2ms -> kernel-run 4.1ms -> total 178ms.
- CUPTI shows kernel queue depth hitting >64 pending shortly before the dispatch stall in slow traces.
- perf counters on NVLINK_PORT show 3x higher retried-packets metric during spikes.

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) NVLink congestion and retries cause inter-GPU copy to prolong and indirectly cause GPU stream serialization (high confidence). Evidence: per-port counters, co-scheduled neighbor pod activity, and high nvlink copy times.
2) Runtime's single-stream submission pattern for small kernels results in queue buildup when copy stalls; if a copy blocks the DMA engine, kernels wait on stream and GPU-side serialization amplifies effect (medium-high confidence).
3) CPU-side threadpool starvation: when many small requests arrive, grpc thread reuse + Python GIL stall the dispatcher, nudging submit latencies up (medium confidence).
4) Kernel fusion mis-scheduling: fused kernels can be split across streams unexpectedly causing extra cross-stream barriers (low-medium confidence).

Repro steps (manual):
1) Synthetic microbench: launch 4 concurrent copy-heavy jobs (nvlink peer-to-peer memcpy loop) on neighbor partition while running single-client generation traces. Observe p95 jump.
2) Instrumented traces: add extra spans around runtime.copy_to_peer and runtime.enqueue_kernel and collect CUPTI traces.
3) Controlled: run everything on exclusive host (no neighbor pods) -> p95 tail collapses by ~55% on average for large seq.

Quick mitigation ideas (short-term):
- Prefer async memcpy + overlap heuristics: prioritize kernel dispatch over non-critical NVLink copies when queue depth > threshold. (patch candidate)
- Introduce NVLink-aware routing policy: prefer models / pods to be placed to avoid heavy simultaneous peer-copy patterns (sched rule / placement constraint).
- Increase runtime submission parallelism: use multiple CUDA streams per request to reduce single-stream blocking (careful: may increase kernel contention).
- Add a backpressure cap: if nvlink copy latency > X ms, switch to local-only KV fallback or degrade to a smaller model variant to avoid tail amplification.

Longer-term engineering experiments / tasks:
- Measure whether NCCL or driver-level settings (e.g., enabling aggressive flow control or lane rebalancing) reduce retries.
- Add runtime-level dynamic sharding to reduce peer-copy volume for large KV updates (shard KV updates and apply asynchronously).
- Explore hardware isolation: test on host types with different NVLink topologies (pairwise vs mesh) to measure topology sensitivity.
- Consider an on-host fabric QoS shim (if cloud partner provides) to isolate NVLink heavy tenants.

Open questions / unknowns to validate:
- Are there specific model shapes (attention config / kv layout) that amplify peer-copy volume?
- Does enabling kernel fusion predictably change the tail shape (we saw mixed results across experiments)?
- What's the minimal runtime change to prefer kernel execution over peer-copy without regressions in throughput?

Immediate next actions (who/when):
- Maya: land small submit-parallelism experiment (multiple submission streams with a toggle) on a canary pool by 2026-02-28. (PR: GHD-3124)
- Ethan: run NVLink microbench across three host types and capture perf counters; deliver dataset by 2026-03-05.
- Rita: prototype placement constraint to avoid colocating copy-heavy workloads; test in staging by 2026-03-10.

Notes to reviewers:
- Traces attached in /artifacts/traces/nvlink-jitter-2026-02.tar (link in linked_artifacts above).
- This doc is a working log — lots of rough traces and TODOs. Final recommendations will consolidate after the canary experiments.

Scratch / misc observations:
- Some p99 traces have short (~5ms) bursts in egress due to TCP retransmits when emitter is streaming many small chunks — might be related to Nagle/tcp_sack settings. Worth looking into separately.
- Observed occasional kernel slowdown on GPU when temperature > 78C; correlate with host-level cooling logs.

Unresolved immediate block: we need a reproducible unit test that reproduces NVLink retried-packet spikes in CI. If we can reproduce, we can add regression tests to prevent regressions.
